MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 2 Technology and Attention Digital technology makes information easy to access, but access does not guarantee deep understanding. Constantly shifting attention can lead to superficial processing. Digital tools are not inherently harmful: when used deliberately, they can support learning through note-taking, source comparison, and returning to difficult sections. The important distinction is between using technology as a tool and allowing it to control the rhythm of attention. Better digital habits therefore require control over how and when technology is used. 1. The central idea is that: A. technology should be rejected B. access guarantees understanding C. deliberate technology use matters more than access alone D. online learning is impossible E. headlines are sufficient 2. Repeated interruptions may cause: A. deeper analysis B. superficial processing C. better memory D. greater concentration E. faster comprehension 3. The author\003s attitude is: A. completely negative B. uncritically positive C. balanced D. fearful E. indifferent 4. Which is deliberate use? A. checking headlines constantly B. moving between articles C. taking notes and revisiting difficult sections D. collecting headlines E. avoiding all devices 5. \004Dictate the rhythm of attention\005 means: A. control when and how attention shifts B. improve handwriting C. block information D. slow reading E. remove attention 6. Which inference is supported? A. Information quantity alone does not ensure learning. B. Online learning is always inferior. C. Interruptions improve memory. D. Technology has no educational value. E. Only students have attention problems. 7. The author would agree that: A. devices should be abandoned B. digital tools are useful when intentional C. headlines are better than articles D. deep learning is impossible online

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 3 E. schools should ban technology 8. Which is NOT mentioned? A. note-taking B. comparing sources C. revisiting difficult sections D. reading long articles E. memorising headlines 9. The passage contrasts: A. students and teachers B. books and technology C. information access and depth of understanding D. schools and homes E. speed and memory 10. Best title: A. The End of Digital Learning B. Technology, Attention and Deliberate Use C. Why Headlines Are Dangerous D. Learning Without Information E. The History of the Internet

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 4 Urban Trees Urban trees provide more than decoration. They can give shade, reduce heat, intercept some rainwater, and create habitats. Their benefits depend on planning. Trees need sufficient root space, suitable species, adequate soil, and regular maintenance. Therefore, urban programmes should not simply maximize tree numbers. They should create healthy and sustainable environments that fit surrounding infrastructure. 11. The main point is: A. trees are decorative B. cities need planning, not merely more trees C. trees should only be in parks D. maintenance is unnecessary E. trees have few benefits 12. Which benefit is NOT mentioned? A. shade B. rainwater interception C. habitats D. heat reduction E. drinking water 13. Poor species selection may: A. increase maintenance costs B. remove wildlife C. prevent rainfall D. guarantee pavement damage E. stop all growth 14. Tone: A. analytical and practical B. sarcastic C. angry D. humorous E. celebratory 15. Increasing tree numbers without planning may: A. create avoidable problems B. always improve cities C. eliminate maintenance D. reduce biodiversity E. solve infrastructure issues 16. \004At any cost\005 suggests: A. without considering consequences B. for free C. with government funding D. during emergencies E. after planning 17. What is specifically necessary? A. adequate soil B. expensive lighting C. tall buildings D. private ownership E. tourist demand

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 5 18. The author distinguishes between: A. birds and trees B. parks and streets C. quantity and sustainable planning D. rain and heat E. cities and villages 19. Which is supported? A. Every species thrives anywhere. B. Urban trees require context-sensitive planning. C. Maintenance is unnecessary. D. Trees have no practical benefits. E. More trees solve every problem. 20. Best title: A. Trees as Urban Infrastructure B. The Problem with Birds C. Why Cities Need More Roads D. The Cost of Rain E. Decorating Modern Streets

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 6 The Value of Failure Failure is not automatically valuable, but unsuccessful attempts can provide information. A failed experiment may reveal an incorrect assumption, while an unsuccessful business idea may reveal weak market response. If mistakes are repeated without analysis, little is learned. Useful failure involves reflection, revision, and another attempt with better information. Failure becomes useful when reflection converts an unsuccessful result into knowledge. 21. The central argument is that failure: A. is always better B. is useful when examined C. should always be avoided D. guarantees success E. has no link to knowledge 22. A failed experiment may: A. reveal an incorrect assumption B. guarantee funding C. remove uncertainty D. replace analysis E. prove success 23. Repeated failure without analysis: A. teaches little B. guarantees resilience C. is ideal D. guarantees innovation E. is better than success 24. Tone: A. reflective and analytical B. mocking C. pessimistic D. hostile E. comic 25. \004Resilient\005 refers to people who: A. avoid challenges B. recover and adapt after setbacks C. never change D. ignore mistakes E. depend on luck 26. What converts failure into knowledge? A. disappointment B. repetition alone C. reflection and revision D. praise E. speed 27. Which is NOT supported? A. failure can provide information B. analysis matters C. every failure is automatically valuable D. approaches can be revised

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 7 E. assumptions can be revealed 28. Success and failure can both be: A. complete opposites B. sources of information C. equally disappointing D. unrelated to learning E. identical 29. \004Better information\005 implies: A. future attempts can use previous experience B. information prevents all mistakes C. failure should be hidden D. only successful people have information E. analysis is unnecessary 30. Best title: A. Failure as a Source of Learning B. Why Success Is Impossible C. The Science of Luck D. Avoiding Every Mistake E. The End of Experimentation

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 8 Public Transport and Choice Improving public transport is not simply a matter of adding buses or trains. Reliability, frequency, safety, convenience, and access to stations affect travel choices. An inexpensive but unpredictable system may be less attractive than a slightly more expensive dependable one. Affordability remains important, especially for lower-income commuters. Transport policy should therefore consider the overall passenger experience, including reliable service, connected routes, safe stations, and convenient ticketing. 31. Demand depends on: A. capacity alone B. the overall travel experience C. price alone D. stations only E. advertising 32. Which is NOT listed? A. reliability B. safety C. frequency D. ticketing convenience E. restaurant quality 33. Why may an inexpensive unpredictable system be less attractive? A. Passengers value reliability too. B. Passengers dislike low prices. C. It has too many trains. D. Safety is irrelevant. E. It always has fewer routes. 34. Tone: A. practical and balanced B. sarcastic C. emotional D. dismissive E. humorous 35. Affordability: A. is irrelevant B. remains important, especially for lower-income commuters C. matters only to tourists D. should be eliminated E. always matters more than reliability 36. \004Overall\005 emphasizes: A. one feature B. the combined travel experience C. ticket prices only D. number of buses E. architecture 37. Suggested alongside capacity increases: A. less safety B. better ticketing convenience C. fewer routes D. unpredictability

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 9 E. lower frequency 38. The passage challenges the idea that: A. transport matters B. adding capacity alone is sufficient C. safety matters D. price matters E. people choose transport 39. Reasonable inference: A. attractiveness can improve without only expanding capacity B. cost never matters C. more buses always reduce demand D. safety has no role E. convenience is irrelevant 40. Best title: A. Beyond Capacity: What Makes Public Transport Attractive B. Why Buses Are Expensive C. The History of Ticketing D. Transport Without Passengers E. The Problem with Stations

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 10 Reading and Memory Exam reading requires identifying structure, distinguishing central claims from examples, and making supported inferences. Trying to memorize every sentence consumes time and may obscure the overall argument. A better approach is to build a mental map: understand the subject, note each paragraph\003s role, and return to the passage when a question asks for a specific detail. This combines comprehension with selective retrieval and reduces the temptation to answer from general knowledge. 41. The passage recommends: A. memorising every sentence B. structured reading and selective retrieval C. avoiding details D. using general knowledge E. reading only the first paragraph 42. A reader should identify: A. only words B. structure and central claims C. author biography D. every sentence E. outside facts 43. Memorising every detail can: A. guarantee errors B. consume time and obscure the argument C. make reading faster D. eliminate inference E. solve all questions 44. A \004mental map\005 means: A. a city map B. understanding subject and paragraph roles C. a word list D. outside facts E. an answer key 45. Return to the passage when: A. every question is answered B. a question requires a specific detail C. you know nothing D. the passage is short E. the test ends 46. A legitimate inference must: A. come from imagination B. be reasonably supported by the passage C. use outside knowledge D. contradict the passage E. be complicated 47. The passage warns against: A. selective retrieval B. structure C. paragraph roles D. answering from general knowledge

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 11 E. returning to text 48. Tone: A. instructional and practical B. angry C. comic D. uncertain E. hostile 49. Selective retrieval means: A. memorising everything B. locating relevant information when needed C. ignoring the passage D. guessing E. reading without purpose 50. Best title: A. A Practical Method for Exam Reading B. Why Memorization Always Wins C. Reading Only for Pleasure D. How to Avoid Reading E. General Knowledge in Exams

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 12 Habit and Environment Habits are often described as matters of willpower, but the surrounding environment can influence repeated behaviour. A phone beside a study book creates different cues from a phone kept elsewhere. Keeping healthy food visible can make it easier to choose. Making an undesirable activity inconvenient can reduce its frequency. Personal discipline remains relevant, but changing the environment can reduce the effort needed to act according to an intention. Habit change can therefore involve arranging surroundings so desired actions become easier and undesired actions require more deliberate effort. 51. Habits are influenced by: A. willpower alone B. environment and discipline C. food prices only D. technology only E. luck 52. Environmental changes can: A. make desired actions easier B. remove discipline C. guarantee success D. eliminate habits instantly E. prevent learning 53. The phone example illustrates: A. cues B. memory C. income D. weather E. age 54. Personal discipline is: A. irrelevant B. relevant but not the only factor C. harmful D. impossible E. the only solution 55. An undesirable activity may be reduced by: A. making it convenient B. requiring more deliberate effort C. placing cues beside it D. removing alternatives E. ignoring surroundings 56. \004Surrounding a person\005 means: A. the context around them B. their personality C. their score D. their history E. their income 57. Which is NOT an example? A. phone placement B. food visibility C. inconvenience D. weather

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 13 E. healthy food 58. Habit change can involve: A. designing surroundings intentionally B. avoiding all decisions C. only motivation D. ignoring cues E. eliminating routines 59. Tone: A. practical and explanatory B. sarcastic C. hostile D. dramatic E. dismissive 60. Best title: A. Designing the Environment for Better Habits B. Why Discipline Is Useless C. The History of Phones D. Food and Motivation E. Habits Without Choices

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 14 Scientific Communication Scientific knowledge becomes more useful when findings are communicated clearly. Technical precision is necessary, but precision does not require unnecessary complexity. A researcher can explain a result in language suited to the audience without changing the evidence. Problems arise when communication exaggerates certainty or hides limitations. Responsible explanation distinguishes what evidence shows from what remains uncertain. Clear scientific communication therefore preserves accuracy while making reasoning accessible. 61. Scientific communication should be: A. complex B. accurate and accessible C. simplified regardless of evidence D. certain only E. free of limitations 62. Precision does NOT require: A. accuracy B. appropriate language C. unnecessary complexity D. evidence E. clear reasoning 63. Limitations should be communicated to: A. preserve responsible interpretation B. make research impossible C. increase certainty D. hide evidence E. avoid audiences 64. The author criticizes communication that: A. explains clearly B. matches audience C. exaggerates certainty D. preserves evidence E. shows uncertainty 65. \004Underlying evidence\005 means: A. evidence supporting the result B. salary C. audience opinion D. paper title E. unrelated facts 66. What must be preserved? A. accuracy B. complexity C. uncertainty only D. jargon E. length 67. Simplification is acceptable when it: A. changes evidence B. preserves accuracy C. removes limitations D. adds certainty

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 RC Mock Test 1 Page 15 E. hides reasoning 68. Tone: A. analytical and responsible B. comic C. angry D. dismissive E. fearful 69. Which is supported? A. Clear communication can improve understanding without changing evidence. B. Complex language is always more accurate. C. Uncertainty should be hidden. D. Researchers should avoid public communication. E. Communication is only vocabulary simplification. 70. Best title: A. Accuracy and Accessibility in Scientific Communication B. Why Science Must Be Complicated C. Removing Uncertainty from Research D. The End of Scientific Evidence E. Vocabulary in Science

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 2 PASSAGE 1 - The Efficiency Paradox Efficiency is usually praised because it allows more to be achieved with fewer resources. Yet efficiency can create a hidden weakness when a system is optimized too narrowly. A company that keeps almost no spare inventory may reduce storage costs, for example, but it may also become vulnerable when deliveries are disrupted. Similarly, an organization that schedules every employee at maximum capacity may appear productive while leaving little room to respond to an unexpected demand. The lesson is not that inefficiency is desirable. Rather, a robust system may deliberately preserve some unused capacity because resilience has value that ordinary efficiency calculations can overlook. What seems wasteful from the perspective of a single moment may prove valuable when conditions change. 1. The central argument is that: A. efficiency is always harmful B. unused capacity can sometimes strengthen resilience C. companies should maximize inventory D. productivity is impossible to measure E. unexpected demand is rare 2. The inventory example illustrates that: A. lower storage costs eliminate all risk B. narrow optimization may increase vulnerability C. inventory is never useful D. deliveries are always predictable E. storage costs are irrelevant 3. Why may maximum employee scheduling create weakness? A. It guarantees low morale. B. It leaves little room to respond to unexpected demand. C. It reduces all productivity. D. It increases inventory. E. It eliminates planning. 4. The author does NOT argue that: A. efficiency can have hidden costs B. resilience may require some spare capacity C. inefficiency is always desirable D. systems can be optimized too narrowly E. conditions can change 5. The phrase "optimized too narrowly" most nearly means: A. designed around a limited objective without broader risks B. made physically smaller C. improved by many teams D. planned without deadlines E. reduced to zero 6. Which inference is best supported? A. A system designed only for average conditions may struggle during disruptions. B. More unused capacity always produces better outcomes. C. Efficiency and resilience can never coexist. D. Inventory should always be maximized. E. Unexpected events can be fully predicted. 7. The author's tone is: A. balanced and cautionary B. sarcastic C. celebratory

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 3 D. hostile E. uncertain 8. What do ordinary efficiency calculations overlook? A. the value of resilience B. the cost of storage C. employee schedules D. delivery times E. productivity measures 9. Which statement would the author most likely agree with? A. Some apparent slack can be an intentional form of protection. B. Every unused resource is waste. C. Resilience has no economic value. D. Businesses should avoid efficiency. E. Only large companies need spare capacity. 10. Best title: A. When Efficiency Needs a Safety Margin B. Why Efficiency Always Fails C. The End of Productivity D. Inventory Management Basics E. How to Eliminate Spare Capacity

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 4 PASSAGE 2 - Expertise and Explanation Experts often know far more about a subject than they realize they know. Because some concepts have become automatic to them, they can underestimate how difficult those concepts are for beginners. This is one reason expert explanation can fail even when the speaker is highly knowledgeable. Effective teaching requires more than possessing correct information; it requires recognizing which steps are invisible to a novice and making those steps explicit. The best explanations therefore do not necessarily contain the most information. They contain the information needed at the right level, in an order the learner can follow. Expertise becomes educationally useful when knowledge is reorganized for another person's understanding. 11. The main idea is that effective explanation requires experts to: A. display maximum knowledge B. make hidden steps explicit C. avoid simplifying anything D. use technical vocabulary E. teach only advanced concepts 12. Experts may underestimate difficulty because: A. they dislike beginners B. some concepts have become automatic C. they lack information D. beginners know too much E. teaching is always easy 13. According to the passage, effective teaching requires: A. only accurate information B. recognizing invisible steps and presenting them clearly C. maximizing the amount of material D. avoiding structure E. speaking as quickly as possible 14. "At the right level" suggests that information should be: A. appropriate to the learner current understanding B. as advanced as possible C. kept secret D. reduced to slogans E. identical for every audience 15. Which statement is NOT supported? A. Experts can overlook beginner difficulties. B. Good explanations need structure. C. More information is always better. D. Teaching may require reorganizing knowledge. E. Automatic knowledge can be invisible to experts. 16. The passage implies that expertise alone: A. guarantees good teaching B. is insufficient for effective teaching C. makes beginners unnecessary D. reduces knowledge E. prevents communication 17. The phrase "reorganized for another person's understanding" implies that: A. the same knowledge may need a different presentation B. experts should change facts C. teachers should omit all difficult ideas D. knowledge has no fixed meaning

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 5 E. beginners should teach experts 18. Author's tone: A. analytical and instructional B. mocking C. emotional D. dismissive E. comic 19. What would most improve an expert's explanation? A. Adding every possible detail B. Identifying steps a novice is likely to miss C. Using more jargon D. Removing all examples E. Avoiding sequence 20. Best title: A. Turning Expertise into Effective Explanation B. Why Experts Know Too Little C. Teaching Without Knowledge D. The Problem with Beginners E. More Information Means Better Teaching

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 6 PASSAGE 3 - The Architecture of Choice People do not make decisions in a vacuum. The way options are arranged can influence which choice appears convenient, visible, or normal. A cafeteria that places fruit near the beginning of a serving line may make fruit easier to select, even without banning less healthy foods. Such design is sometimes called a choice architecture. Critics worry that arranging options can become manipulative, especially when the designer goals are hidden. Supporters argue that all environments already shape behaviour to some extent, so the relevant question is whether that influence is transparent and aligned with people interests. The debate is therefore less about whether choices are influenced and more about how such influence should be exercised. 21. The passage mainly discusses: A. why people lack freedom B. how the arrangement of choices can influence behaviour C. why cafeterias should ban unhealthy foods D. how advertisements work E. why decisions are random 22. What is choice architecture? A. the physical construction of buildings B. the arrangement of options that can influence choices C. a legal voting system D. a method of accounting E. a psychological diagnosis 23. The fruit example shows that: A. ban policies are necessary B. placement can affect convenience and selection C. people dislike fruit D. cafeterias manipulate everyone E. healthy food is always cheaper 24. A criticism mentioned is that choice design may become: A. expensive B. manipulative C. ineffective D. irrelevant E. scientific 25. Supporters argue that: A. environments already influence behaviour B. all manipulation is harmless C. people never have preferences D. choices should be hidden E. food should be regulated 26. The debate is mainly about: A. whether influence exists at all B. how influence should be exercised C. whether cafeterias are profitable D. whether people can choose E. whether fruit is healthy 27. Which inference is supported? A. Transparency may matter when designing environments that steer choices. B. Any influence on behaviour is necessarily unethical. C. Choice architecture eliminates freedom.

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 7 D. Hidden goals are always beneficial. E. Only food environments shape decisions. 28. The author's tone is: A. nuanced and balanced B. angry C. sarcastic D. dismissive E. absolute 29. Which statement is NOT consistent with the passage? A. Option arrangement can shape behaviour. B. Designers may have goals. C. Critics worry about manipulation. D. All decisions are completely independent of context. E. Supporters see some influence as unavoidable. 30. Best title: A. How the Design of Options Shapes Choice B. Why Choice Is Impossible C. The Science of Cafeterias D. Banning Unhealthy Foods E. Decision-Making Without Context

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 8 PASSAGE 4 - Memory and Reconstruction Human memory is not a perfect recording system. Remembering involves reconstruction, meaning that a person may retain the general outline of an event while particular details are altered over time. This does not make every memory false. It does mean that confidence in a memory and accuracy of that memory are not necessarily identical. New information, repeated retelling, and expectations can influence what is later recalled. For this reason, a vivid recollection should not automatically be treated as precise evidence. A careful approach asks how the memory was formed, what information may have been introduced later, and whether independent evidence supports the recollection. 31. The central claim is that memory: A. is always false B. records events perfectly C. is reconstructive and can be influenced over time D. has no value E. becomes more accurate when vivid 32. The passage distinguishes between: A. memory and attention B. confidence and accuracy C. events and expectations D. evidence and knowledge E. time and place 33. A vivid memory should NOT automatically be treated as: A. evidence at all B. precise evidence C. an event D. a recollection E. a possibility 34. What can influence later recall? A. only age B. new information, retelling, and expectations C. nothing after the event D. independent evidence only E. weather 35. The phrase reconstruction suggests that remembering: A. replays a perfect recording B. can involve rebuilding details from stored information C. is impossible D. depends only on confidence E. never changes 36. Which inference is strongest? A. Independent evidence can help evaluate a confident recollection. B. Confidence proves accuracy. C. All vivid memories are unreliable. D. Memory has no practical use. E. Retelling always improves accuracy. 37. The author's tone is: A. cautious and analytical B. celebratory C. sarcastic D. hostile

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 9 E. comic 38. Which is NOT suggested as a careful approach? A. examining how memory formed B. considering later information C. checking independent evidence D. assuming confidence equals accuracy E. asking what may have changed 39. What does "not necessarily identical" mean? A. confidence and accuracy can differ B. they are always opposite C. they are always equal D. accuracy is irrelevant E. confidence is impossible 40. Best title: A. Why Memory Requires Careful Interpretation B. Memory Is Always False C. The Power of Confidence D. How to Forget Events E. Why Evidence Is Unnecessary

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 10 PASSAGE 5 - Innovation and Constraints Innovation is often associated with freedom: more resources, more options, and fewer restrictions are expected to produce more ideas. Yet constraints can sometimes stimulate creativity. A limited budget may force a team to simplify a product, while a strict technical requirement may lead engineers to discover a novel approach. Constraints do not automatically produce innovation; excessive restrictions can make experimentation impossible. Their value lies in directing attention toward a specific problem and forcing choices among alternatives. The productive question is therefore not whether constraints are good or bad in themselves, but whether they narrow the problem enough to encourage inventive solutions without closing off meaningful possibilities. 41. The main argument is that: A. constraints always improve creativity B. some constraints can encourage innovation when they remain workable C. freedom prevents creativity D. budgets have no effect on design E. restrictions should be unlimited 42. The budget example shows that constraints may: A. force useful simplification B. eliminate all choices C. guarantee innovation D. reduce technical knowledge E. prevent experimentation 43. Excessive restrictions can: A. make experimentation impossible B. guarantee originality C. increase resources D. remove all problems E. improve every solution 44. The value of constraints lies partly in: A. directing attention toward a specific problem B. making choices unlimited C. removing all uncertainty D. eliminating alternatives entirely E. reducing curiosity 45. Meaningful possibilities refers to: A. options still worth exploring B. all possible options in the world C. financial resources D. technical standards E. past ideas 46. Which inference is best supported? A. A useful constraint focuses effort without eliminating discovery. B. The fewer options people have, the better they innovate. C. Creative work needs no experimentation. D. Any strict rule produces originality. E. Innovation requires unlimited funding. 47. The author's tone is: A. balanced and exploratory B. hostile C. absolute

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 11 D. comic E. dismissive 48. The author rejects the simple idea that constraints are: A. always good or always bad B. sometimes useful C. relevant to innovation D. able to focus attention E. capable of becoming excessive 49. Which statement is NOT supported? A. Constraints can simplify problems. B. Technical requirements can spark new approaches. C. Excessive restrictions can be harmful. D. Every constraint automatically creates creativity. E. Innovation depends partly on workable freedom. 50. Best title: A. When Constraints Can Create Creativity B. Why Freedom Destroys Innovation C. Innovation Without Choices D. Budgets and Engineers E. The End of Experimentation

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 12 PASSAGE 6 - The Visibility of Work Some kinds of work are easy to notice because their outputs are visible: a finished building, a published article, or a completed software feature. Other forms of work are less visible, such as maintenance, coordination, checking, and preventing problems before they occur. Organizations that evaluate performance only through visible outputs may therefore undervalue activities that preserve reliability. This can create a strange incentive: workers may prioritize tasks that can be displayed while postponing less visible tasks that are nevertheless essential. A sensible evaluation system should recognize both production and prevention. What matters is not only what was created, but also what failures, delays, or costs were avoided. 51. The passage mainly argues that organizations should: A. measure only visible outputs B. recognize invisible preventive work as well as production C. avoid evaluating workers D. prioritize presentation over reliability E. remove maintenance tasks 52. Which work is described as less visible? A. construction B. publication C. maintenance and coordination D. software creation E. all physical work 53. Why may visible-output-only evaluation create a problem? A. Workers may neglect essential but less visible tasks. B. Workers become more innovative automatically. C. Maintenance becomes easier. D. Visible outputs disappear. E. Prevention becomes profitable. 54. The phrase "strange incentive" refers to: A. pressure to choose what can be displayed B. a reward for preventing failure C. a salary increase D. a technical system E. an unexpected promotion 55. A sensible evaluation system should recognize: A. production and prevention B. only speed C. only results D. only teamwork E. only visible work 56. The final sentence suggests value can be measured by: A. what was created and what was avoided B. only products C. only revenue D. only employee visibility E. only delays 57. Which inference is supported? A. Some important contributions may be overlooked because they leave little visible evidence. B. Invisible work has no measurable value. C. Preventing problems is always more important than producing.

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 13 D. Visible outputs should be ignored. E. Organizations cannot evaluate reliability. 58. The author's tone is: A. practical and critical B. sarcastic C. angry D. celebratory E. uncertain 59. Which is NOT mentioned as less visible activity? A. checking B. coordination C. maintenance D. preventing problems E. advertising 60. Best title: A. Measuring the Work You Cannot Easily See B. Why Visible Work Is Always Better C. The End of Maintenance D. Producing Without Prevention E. How to Display Every Task

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 14 PASSAGE 7 - Cities and Informal Knowledge Urban planning often relies on maps, statistics, and formal surveys, but residents possess another type of information: practical knowledge gained from repeated experience of a place. Residents may know which path floods after heavy rain, where traffic becomes difficult at a particular hour, or which public space feels unsafe after dark. Such knowledge is not automatically complete or unbiased, but neither is it irrelevant simply because it is informal. Planning improves when local experience is combined with systematic evidence. The challenge is to collect resident observations in a way that can be compared, verified, and incorporated into larger planning decisions without treating every individual account as universally representative. 61. The central idea is that urban planning should: A. ignore resident experience B. use informal local knowledge alongside systematic evidence C. replace data with anecdotes D. trust every resident claim E. avoid surveys 62. Residents may know: A. only official statistics B. practical patterns not captured easily by formal tools C. all city history D. future traffic conditions with certainty E. every unsafe location 63. The author says resident knowledge is: A. always unbiased B. always complete C. not automatically complete or unbiased, but potentially useful D. irrelevant E. better than all formal evidence 64. What is the challenge in using informal knowledge? A. Collecting it so it can be compared and verified B. Preventing residents from speaking C. Removing all statistics D. Treating every account as universally representative E. Avoiding local observations 65. Universally representative means: A. applicable to everyone or the whole area B. verified by science C. easy to collect D. legally required E. historically accurate 66. Which inference is best supported? A. Local observations can add value when integrated carefully rather than accepted uncritically. B. Formal evidence is unnecessary. C. Every resident sees the city identically. D. Anecdotes should replace maps. E. Informal knowledge is always superior. 67. The author's tone is: A. inclusive and cautious B. dismissive C. hostile

MHT-CET MBA/MMS - Reading Comprehension Mock Test 2 Page 15 D. sarcastic E. absolute 68. Which is NOT an example of local practical knowledge? A. flood-prone paths B. traffic at a particular hour C. unsafe-feeling spaces D. official census totals E. repeated experience 69. Why should resident accounts not automatically be treated as universal? A. Individual experiences may not represent the whole area. B. Residents never observe patterns. C. Formal surveys are always perfect. D. Local knowledge is illegal. E. Cities have no patterns. 70. Best title: A. Combining Local Experience with Urban Data B. Why Maps Should Be Rejected C. The Problem with Residents D. Statistics Without Streets E. Planning Without Evidence

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 VA Sectional Mock 1 Page 8 PART 7 \001 READING COMPREHENSION Organisations often measure what is easiest to count: calls completed, tasks closed, or products delivered. These measures can be useful, but they provide only a partial picture of performance. A team may close many tasks while creating avoidable errors that another team must repair. Similarly, a support desk may answer calls quickly without resolving customers\005 underlying problems. When a measure becomes the sole target, people may prioritise the measured activity over less visible work. This does not mean that metrics should be abandoned. Instead, they should be interpreted alongside quality, long-term outcomes, and evidence about unintended effects. A sound evaluation system uses numbers as clues about performance, not as a complete definition of it. 44. What is the central idea of the passage? A. Organisations should stop measuring performance. B \002 when the power Explanation (Hinglish): Standard pair \003no sooner\010than\004 hai, \003no sooner\010when\004 nahi. 24. E \002 No error Explanation (Hinglish): Sentence grammatically aur logically correct hai. 25. B \002 Accommodation Explanation (Hinglish): Correct spelling accommodation: double c aur double m. 26. C \002 Maintenance Explanation (Hinglish): Correct spelling maintenance; word family maintain \011 maintenance. 29. B \002 Occurrence Explanation (Hinglish): Occurrence mein double c aur double r aata hai. 30. B \002 Privilege Explanation (Hinglish): Correct spelling privilege; extra d nahi hota. 31. A \002 Q\006S\006P\006R Explanation (Hinglish): Question define (Q), data collect (S), results compare (P), phir conclusion (R). 32. B \002 S\006Q\006R\006P Explanation (Hinglish): S problem introduce karta hai, Q investigation, R solution, P result. Order S\006Q\006R\006P. 33. A \002 Q\006R\006P\006S Explanation (Hinglish): Q problem, R edit, P immediate benefit (\003This\004), S later outcome. 34. A \002 Q\006P\006R\006S Explanation (Hinglish): Q programme, P initial limitation, R response, S improvement. 35. A \002 Q\006P\006R\006S Explanation (Hinglish): Q defects discover, P launch postpone, R defects fix, S final test schedule. 36. A \002 Q\006P\006S\006R Explanation (Hinglish): Q problem, P response, S explains how review helped, R outcome. 37. B \002 A new software system was introduced at the same time and automated routine tasks. Explanation (Hinglish): Naya software alternative cause ho sakta hai. Productivity rise training ki wajah se hi hui, yeh claim weaken hota hai. 38. B \002 Poor visibility contributes to at least some nighttime accidents. Explanation (Hinglish): Agar poor visibility kuch accidents ka factor hai tab lights se reduction ka argument banta hai. 39. C \002 Frequent customers are more likely to sign up for the card in the first place. Explanation (Hinglish): Ho sakta hai pehle se frequent customers hi card lete hon. Reverse selection ke kaaran cause establish nahi hota. 40. B \002 Report X underwent peer review. Explanation (Hinglish): Premise directly kehta hai institute ke published reports peer review se guzarte hain; X bhi unmein se hai. 41. B \002 Whether a similar class without the programme improved by a comparable amount. Explanation (Hinglish): Comparison group pata karne se judge hoga improvement programme-specific tha ya general trend. 42. B \002 A review finds teams with shorter, focused meetings complete comparable work with fewer interruptions. Explanation (Hinglish): Comparable work fewer interruptions ke saath complete hona shorter focused meetings ke favour mein evidence hai. 43. B \002 No major service changes occurred, and many new riders said lower fares were their main reason for switching. Explanation (Hinglish): Alternative changes na hona aur riders ka low fare ko main reason batana causal claim ko support karta hai.

MHT-CET MBA/MMS \001 VA Sectional Mock 1 Page 12 44. B \002 Easy-to-count metrics are useful but should not be treated as the whole picture. Explanation (Hinglish): Main point: metrics useful hain, lekin performance ko completely define nahi karte. 45. B \002 People may prioritise the measured activity over less visible work. Explanation (Hinglish): Sole target banne par log usi activity ko prioritise kar sakte hain jo measure hoti hai. 46. B \002 speed alone may not mean the underlying problem is resolved Explanation (Hinglish): Call ka quick answer dena aur customer ki actual problem solve karna alag cheezein hain. 47. C \002 balanced and cautionary Explanation (Hinglish): Author metrics ko reject nahi karta; limitations samjha kar broader evaluation recommend karta hai. 48. B \002 an incomplete view Explanation (Hinglish): Partial picture = incomplete view; performance ka sirf ek hissa capture hota hai. 49. B \002 Numbers should be considered with quality and long-term outcomes. Explanation (Hinglish): Passage mein metrics ko quality aur long-term outcomes ke saath interpret karne ko kaha gaya hai. 50. B \002 When Metrics Do Not Tell the Whole Story Explanation (Hinglish): Yeh title passage ke overall theme ko capture karta hai: metrics useful hain, but complete picture nahi.

Pehle Task 1 ke detailed vocabulary notes ko recall karna hai, phir Vocabulary + Grammar mixed practice karni hai. LR, AR aur QA ko aaj hold par rakha gaya hai because current topic-wise phase mein Vocabulary ko strong banana priority hai. 1. Vocabulary Revision \001 Task 1 45\00150 minutes. \002 List of Words: minimum 25 words. Meaning + Hinglish meaning + 1 example + synonym/antonym recall karo. \002 Confused & Misused: Affect/Effect, Accept/Except, Advice/Advise, Principal/Principle, Stationary/Stationery, Compliment/Complement, Loose/Lose, Then/Than, Their/There/They're, Your/You're, Its/It's, Desert/Dessert, Elicit/Illicit, Fewer/Less, Wary/Weary. \002 Phobias + Manias: root dekhkar term identify karo. \002 Prefixes/Suffixes: un-, dis-, in-/im-/il-/ir-, re-, pre-, post-, anti-, auto-, bi-, tri-, mis-, co-, sub-, super-, inter-, trans-. \002 Analogies: synonym, antonym, person-workplace, person-tool, object-function, part-whole, young-adult, material-product, cause-effect, degree/intensity and group relations. 2. Vocabulary Recall \001 30 Questions Notes band karke: 10 meaning/synonym/antonym + 8 confused words + 4 phobias/manias + 4 prefixes/suffixes + 4 analogies. Target: 24/30+ . Wrong/doubtful words ko \000 mark karo. 3. Grammar Revision \001 20 Questions Completed grammar topics se revise karo: Articles, Nouns, Pronouns, Adjectives . Then 20 questions attempt karo, especially correct usage and basic error spotting. Target: 15/20+ . Har wrong answer ka one-line reason likho. 4. Timed Practice \001 30 Questions / 25 Minutes No notes, no pause. 18 Vocabulary + 12 Grammar. All 30 attempt karne hain. Target accuracy: 75%+ . Timer ke baad mistakes ko classify karo: Meaning / Confusion / Grammar Rule / Analogy / Careless Error. 5. What to Revise After Practice \002 All \000 words. \002 Confused pairs jahan difference clear nahi tha. \002 5 analogies that took more than 45 seconds. \002 All wrong grammar questions. \002 3 words you recognised but could not use correctly in a sentence. 6. Difficulty Rule Aaj ka goal maximum new content nahi, recall + accuracy improve karna hai. Timed block 75% se kam hua to next day difficulty same rakhenge. 80\00185%+ hua to tougher vocabulary and mixed questions add karenge. 7. 5-Line Progress Check # Report What to send

1 Topics completed Aaj kya actually complete hua? 2 Questions attempted Total attempted / 80 3 Correct answers Correct / attempted 4 Accuracy + time Accuracy % + timed block ka actual time 5 Doubts Difficult words, pairs, grammar rules, analogies CET Pattern Note The latest official MAH-MBA/MMS-CET 2026 brochure states: 150 minutes , questions in English , five options with one correct answer , and no negative marking . The CET Cell currently lists the MBA/MMS CET A.Y. 2026\00127 brochure. No 2027 exam date is assumed. \000cite\000turn0search12\000turn0search1\000 Why no LR/AR/QA today? \001 Mark any question taking over 90 seconds. 20 Verbal Ability / RC Focus: Vocabulary + Sentence-level English.
\001 Revise 20 studied words.
\001 Revise 10 confused/misused pairs.
\001 10 Vocabulary questions.
\001 5 sentence-completion/appropriate-word questions.
\001 Note 5 uncertain words/pairs. 15 Timed Practice Block \001 30 Minutes 30 questions in 30 minutes, one sitting. LR: 8 questions / 8 min \001 AR: 5 / 5 min \001 QA: 8 / 9 min \001 VA/Vocabulary: 9 / 8 min. Stop when the timer ends and record the score. Target: Attempt all 30. The official 2026 CET has no negative marking, so build the habit of making a best attempt rather than leaving questions unnecessarily blank. What to Revise 1. LR \002 Coding-Decoding patterns and Blood Relation family-tree logic. 2. AR \002 Series rules, movement/rotation, counting and symmetry checks. 3. QA \002 Percentage conversions, percentage change, ratio simplification and proportion setup. 4. VA \002 Today's 20 vocabulary words + 10 confused/misused pairs. 5. Analyse every wrong/guessed question and write why the approach failed. Today's Minimum Target 70 questions total including the timed block. Aim for 75%+ accuracy . If accuracy is below 75%, prioritise error analysis over adding extra questions. 5-Line Progress Check \001 Send This Back 1. Topics completed: ________ 2. Questions attempted: ______ / 70 3. Correct answers: ______ / 70 4. Accuracy + timed-block score/time: ______ 5. Doubts / difficult topics / questions: ________ Official CET Note The latest official MAH-MBA/MMS-CET 2026 brochure specifies 75 Logical Reasoning, 25 Abstract Reasoning, 50 Quantitative Aptitude and 50 Verbal Ability/Reading Comprehension questions: 200 questions in 150 minutes, five options per MCQ, and no negative marking. No 2027 exam date is assumed. Source: Maharashtra State CET Cell \002 MAH-MBA/MMS-CET 2026 Information Brochure (A.Y. 2026\00327).
